title: Sizing a container for production
prompt_md: These are the container decisions that only bite in production: memory ceilings, attacker-controlled input sizes, and caches that grow without bound. Each question describes a running service.

questions.stem_md: A nightly reconciliation job takes 90 seconds on 50 000 orders. Its hot loop does `if order.ref in open_refs:` where `open_refs` is a list that grows with the order count. Traffic is forecast to grow 10× this year. What runtime should capacity planning assume, and why?

options.md: About 2.5 hours — both `n` and `m` grow 10×, so a quadratic path costs roughly 100× more.
About 15 minutes — 10× the data is 10× the time.
About 20 minutes — sorting effects mean growth is n log n.
Unchanged — the job is I/O bound, so CPU complexity does not matter.

questions.explanation_md: Both loop bounds scale with order volume, so the cost is quadratic in a single growth factor: 90 s × 100 ≈ 150 minutes. This is the value of stating complexity in business terms — "quadratic in orders per day" turns a growth forecast directly into a batch-window breach, and the fix (`set(open_refs)` once) returns it to 15 minutes.

sources.locator: list — x in s is O(n)

questions.stem_md: An export endpoint does `rows = [transform(r) for r in cursor]` then serialises `rows`. It has run for a year and is now OOM-killed on the largest tenant. What is the correct fix?

options.md: Stream: make `transform` a generator expression and write incrementally, so peak memory is one row rather than all rows.
Double the container memory limit.
Wrap the comprehension in `try/except MemoryError` and retry.
Call `gc.collect()` before building the list.

questions.explanation_md: The list is O(n) in a tenant-controlled `n`, so any fixed memory limit is eventually exceeded — raising it buys time, not correctness. Replacing the accumulator with a generator makes peak memory independent of row count. `MemoryError` is rarely catchable usefully (the OOM killer sends SIGKILL, which no handler sees) and `gc.collect()` cannot free objects you are still holding.

questions.stem_md: A public JSON endpoint accepts a list of ids and returns matches. Which of these are genuine denial-of-service exposures that a container or algorithm change alone does **not** remove?

options.md: The request body has no size limit, so a caller can post ten million ids.
The handler builds a `set` from the posted ids before matching.
Nested groups in the payload are parsed recursively with no depth limit.
Each id is validated with a regex that backtracks catastrophically on crafted input.
Results are returned in insertion order using `dict.fromkeys`.

questions.explanation_md: Unbounded size, unbounded depth and super-linear regex behaviour are all attacker-controlled cost, and no amount of algorithmic tuning removes the class — the input must be bounded at the boundary (max body size, max item count, max nesting depth, a linear-time matcher). Building a `set` and preserving order with `dict.fromkeys` are both linear and harmless.

questions.stem_md: A service memoises a per-customer lookup with `@functools.cache`. Latency improves immediately; memory climbs steadily for weeks until the pod restarts. What changed the failure mode?

options.md: `functools.cache` is unbounded, so the cache is O(distinct customers) — a time problem was traded for a memory leak.
The cache is thread-local, so each worker keeps a duplicate copy.
Memoisation defeats the garbage collector's generational heuristics.
Nothing changed; steady memory growth is normal for a long-running Python process.

questions.explanation_md: `functools.cache` is `lru_cache(maxsize=None)` — it never evicts, so every distinct argument is retained for the process lifetime along with whatever the value references. Use `lru_cache(maxsize=N)` with an N you can multiply by the entry size and defend, and remember that a cache only improves complexity if the hit rate actually holds.

questions.stem_md: A production API has p99 latency four times its p50, and you cannot reproduce it in staging. Which measurement do you reach for first?

options.md: A sampling profiler (py-spy) attached to the live process — near-zero overhead, no restart, no code change.
`cProfile` around the handler in production.
`timeit` on the suspected function.
`tracemalloc` snapshots on every request.

questions.explanation_md: `cProfile` adds 2-5× overhead, which distorts exactly the tail latency you are chasing; `timeit` needs a hypothesis you do not have yet; `tracemalloc` answers a memory question. A sampling profiler observes the real process at real load and names the frames where the time went.

hints.md: For each scenario, first name what `n` is and who controls it. If a caller controls `n`, any super-linear cost is a availability risk rather than a performance nuisance.

Two distinctions do most of the work here: a quadratic where *both* bounds grow with the same quantity multiplies by the square of the growth factor; and O(n) **memory** in an unbounded input is a crash, not a slowdown, so raising a limit is never the fix.

Answers: (1) ~2.5 hours, because 10× on both bounds is ~100×. (2) Stream with a generator so peak memory is one row. (3) Unbounded body size, unbounded nesting depth, and the backtracking regex. (4) `functools.cache` never evicts, so the cache grows with distinct customers — use `lru_cache(maxsize=N)`. (5) A sampling profiler such as py-spy.
